 Abstract
 Natural disasters displace millions of people each year, and effective disaster response requires accurate models of population movement. This study presents DFlee, an agent-based model for flood-induced evacuation built on the Flee framework for conflict-driven displacement. DFlee introduces three key extensions: (i) dynamic integration of evolving, location-specific flood conditions into agent decision-making; (ii) risk-sensitive destination selection accounting for flood severity, shelter inundation risk, and accessibility; and (iii) recession-driven short-term return-to-origin. Synthetic scenarios with recurrence intervals ranging from 10 to over 100 years represent minor and major riverine floods, coastal storm surges, and compound flooding. Validation combines empirical comparison against the 2022 Bauchi flood in Nigeria with behavioural validation of three stylised facts: preference for nearby safe destinations, short-term return to origin as flood conditions improve, and heterogeneous evacuation timing. Across scenarios, approximately 84–91% of evacuees select the nearest safe destination, while returns to origin begin promptly as flood conditions recede, with cumulative returns within the simulated window limited by late-peaking displacement dynamics. These behaviours persist across a tenfold increase in population size, and ARCHER2 experiments simulate 16 million agents in under one minute on a single compute node and around five seconds on 32 nodes, supporting uncertainty quantification, scenario exploration, and humanitarian planning.

 This appendix presents the complete empirical validation results for the 2022 Bauchi flood case study. It includes the full destination-level comparison between observed International Organization for Migration (IOM) Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) data and DFlee simulation outputs (Table  7 ), together with validation plots for the remaining destination sites.  Appendix C stylised facts for validation
 This appendix presents the complete list of stylised facts (SFs) considered for DFlee validation, comprising the three empirically grounded regularities validated in this paper together with hypothesised regularities identified for future testing that form the foundation for evaluating the plausibility of flood-induced displacement models such as DFlee. Table  8 summarises all stylised facts, their behavioural focus, and key references. The three facts validated in the main paper correspond to observed regularities in distance preference (SF-1), rapid post-flood return (SF-2), and heterogeneous evacuation timing (SF-3); the remaining stylised facts will be explored in future model extensions as additional behavioural modules are incorporated.
 Table 8 Stylised facts relevant to flood-induced displacement, their behavioural focus, and key references. Facts highlighted in bold are validated in this paper and are supported by the cited literature; the remaining entries are hypothesised regularities drawn from the behavioural flood-evacuation literature, to be tested in future model extensions. Full size table Appendix D supplementary results for scenarios 1–4
 This appendix presents the detailed results for Scenarios 1 (Minor Riverine), 2 (Major Riverine), 3 (Coastal storm surge), and 4 (Compound flood), which are summarised in the main text. For each scenario, the appendix includes flood progression, evacuation dynamics, origin–destination heatmaps, and validation against the three stylised facts. The corresponding scenario summaries and cross-scenario quantitative comparisons are presented in the Results and Discussion section (Table 3).
 For transparency, we report here the exact magnitudes of the ensemble 95% confidence intervals underlying the stylised-fact figures. Across all eight scenario/scale combinations, the median relative CI on the destination-rank counts (Stylised Fact 1) is 0.77% of the mean, with a maximum of 17.3% occurring only in the highest rank bins containing a few agents on average. For the departure-time ECDFs (Stylised Fact 3), the ensemble CI is narrower than plot resolution, with a maximum band width of 0.0026 in cumulative departed share (i.e. the true ensemble spread at any timestep never exceeds \(\pm 0.0013\) ). For the return-dynamics curves (Stylised Fact 2), the maximum CI half-width across the four scenarios is below 0.0021 in return share.
 Appendix D.1 scenario 1: minor riverine flood event
 This section reports the detailed per-location diagnostics for the Minor Riverine scenario, complementing the stylised-fact validation presented in the main text.
 Fig. 11 Full size image Simulation results of the Minor Riverine flood scenario across six towns over four days (16 timesteps of 6 hours each). Each subplot shows the total number of agents present at each location over time (original residents plus arrived displaced individuals, minus departures), as the ensemble mean across 50 independent simulation replicas (solid line), with the shaded band indicating ±1 standard deviation across replicas. Values at the first timestep reflect the population state after the initial movement step and therefore differ slightly from the initial allocations in Table  5 . The x-axis represents the simulation period (timesteps), and the y-axis represents the number of agents. Different y-axis ranges reflect substantial variation in population size and destination capacity across locations. The concentration of displaced populations in TR highlights DFlee’s behavioural plausibility under minor riverine flooding.
 To complement the arrival plots in Figure  11 , Figure  12 presents a heatmap showing, for each origin town, the number of evacuating agents over time, with superimposed numbers indicating local flood levels at each time step. This integrated view enables direct comparison between displacement and hazard progression, illustrating that higher flood levels correspond to greater evacuation outflows. In DC and DR, sharp evacuation peaks occur as flood levels rise. TL, TC, and TR also exhibit precautionary outflows despite not being inundated, suggesting anticipatory or socially influenced behaviour. Part of the outflow recorded for persistently safe towns additionally reflects the baseline movement probability ( default_movechance \(\,=0.1\) ), which produces a low level of background mobility even in the absence of any hazard; flood-driven evacuation is superimposed on this baseline churn. Overall, the hazard–response coupling highlights three key dynamics: (i) evacuations peak with hazard escalation, (ii) at-risk but unflooded towns still experience precautionary departures, and (iii) persistently safe destinations remain stable and accumulate displaced populations.
 Fig. 12 Full size image Heatmap of evacuations by origin town over time for Scenario 1, with local flood levels overlaid as numbers. Brighter colours indicate larger evacuation outflows, while darker colours represent smaller outflows. The figure shows that evacuation peaks coincide with rising flood levels, precautionary departures occur even in unflooded towns, and persistently safe destinations accumulate displaced populations.
 Additional behavioural diagnostics
 To further analyse evacuation behaviour, Figure  13 presents boxplots of departure times by origin location. The results show that agents from immediately threatened towns (DC and DR) tend to evacuate earlier, with distributions concentrated around the initial rise in flood levels. By contrast, TC displays later and more dispersed departures, reflecting precautionary or socially influenced behaviour in areas not directly inundated. DL, TR, and TL occupy an intermediate position, with departure timing shifting later as flooding progresses. These patterns reinforce the heterogeneity of evacuation timing (SF-3), demonstrating that risk perception, hazard proximity, and social influence combine to produce varied behavioural responses across towns.
 Fig. 13 Full size image Boxplots of evacuation departure times by origin location. Threatened towns (DC, DR) show earlier departures, while the unflooded towns (TL, TC) exhibit delayed and heterogeneous timing.
 Figure  14 illustrates the distribution of return times across six origin locations. The boxplots highlight notable variations in both median and dispersion of return times among these origins. Generally, populations originating from top locations (TL, TC, TR) exhibit shorter and less variable return times, suggesting quicker and more consistent movements back to their initial locations once flood conditions subside. In contrast, agents from the lower origins, particularly DC and DR, show longer and more dispersed return times, indicating delayed and heterogeneous recovery behaviours. This pattern implies that proximity to more severely flooded zones or limited access to safe routes may prolong displacement duration. Overall, the diagram supports Stylised Fact 2 by showing that return dynamics are spatially dependent, with lower-origin populations facing systematically longer return periods.
 Fig. 14 Full size image Boxplots of return times by origin location. Populations from the top locations (TL, TC, TR) exhibit shorter and less variable return times, whereas agents from the origins closest to the river, particularly DC and DR, show longer and more dispersed return times, reflecting their more severe and prolonged flood exposure.
 Appendix D.2 scenario 2: major riverine flood event
 Figure  15 illustrates the temporal progression of the major riverine flood. Unlike Scenario 1, severe flooding develops immediately in DC and DR and subsequently spreads to TL, TC and DL, leaving TR as the only safe location by Day 3. Floodwaters recede during Day 4, after which previously flooded locations regain attractiveness and their populations recover through a combination of return migration and redistribution of displaced agents from elsewhere in the network.
 The resulting evacuation dynamics are shown in Figures  16 and  17 . Early departures are concentrated in DC and DR, followed by larger evacuation flows from TL, TC and DL as flooding expands across the network. Throughout the peak flood period, TR receives the majority of displaced agents owing to its persistent safety. The evacuation heatmap further illustrates the close correspondence between increasing flood severity and evacuation intensity, while also highlighting precautionary departures before some locations become directly flooded. Behavioural validation against the three stylised facts is presented in Figures  18 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 . As in Scenario 1, agents overwhelmingly prefer nearby safe destinations, begin returning to their origin locations as flood conditions improve, and exhibit heterogeneous evacuation timing. These results indicate that the behavioural mechanisms reproduced by DFlee remain consistent under more severe riverine flooding despite the substantially larger and earlier displacement generated by the increased hazard severity.

This major flood event (50-100 year recurrence interval) affects the same spatial configuration as Scenario 1 but with increased severity, resulting in all locations except Top Right (TR) becoming flooded by Day 3. Location colour coding follows the classification system established in Figure 2.

 Appendix D.3 scenario 3: coastal storm surge event
 Figure  23 illustrates the progression of the coastal storm surge over five days. Flooding first affects the exposed coastal towns (TL, ML and DL), before extending inland to MC and DC and eventually affecting all locations except TR. This progressive inland propagation produces a sequence of evacuations that differs from the riverine scenarios, where flooding develops more gradually along the river corridor.
 The resulting evacuation dynamics are shown in Figures  24 and  25 . Coastal towns experience immediate departures following storm surge onset, while central towns evacuate later as floodwaters propagate inland. During the peak flood period, TR functions as the principal refuge and receives the majority of displaced agents. The evacuation heatmap highlights the close correspondence between flood progression and evacuation intensity, together with precautionary departures from locations before direct inundation.
 Validation against the three stylised facts is presented in Figures  26 , 27 , 28 , 29 , 30 . As in the riverine scenarios, evacuees predominantly select nearby safe destinations, begin returning to their origin locations as flood conditions improve, and exhibit heterogeneous evacuation timing despite similar hazard conditions. These results demonstrate that DFlee reproduces the same behavioural mechanisms under rapid-onset coastal flooding while capturing the larger spatial extent and greater displacement associated with storm surge events.

 Appendix D.4 scenario 4: compound flood event
 Figure  31 illustrates the evolution of the compound flood event. Coastal flooding and riverine flooding occur simultaneously, exposing both the coastal towns (TL, ML and DL) and the river-adjacent towns (DC and DR) from the beginning of the simulation. As the two hazards propagate, flooding extends across the network, leaving TR as the only consistently safe location during the peak flood period. Floodwaters gradually recede during Days 4 and 5, after which previously flooded locations regain attractiveness and their populations recover through a combination of return migration and redistribution of displaced agents from elsewhere in the network.
 The resulting evacuation dynamics are shown in Figures  32 and  33 . Concurrent coastal and riverine hazards generate overlapping evacuation flows that temporarily increase population pressure in intermediate locations before displaced agents ultimately converge on TR. Compared with the previous scenarios, the compound flood produces the most spatially extensive and persistent displacement. The evacuation heatmap further illustrates the close relationship between hazard progression and evacuation intensity throughout the event.
 Validation against the three stylised facts is presented in Figures  34 , 35 , 36 , 37 , 38 . As in the previous scenarios, evacuees predominantly select nearby safe destinations whenever these are available, begin returning to their origin locations as flood conditions improve, and exhibit heterogeneous evacuation timing despite similar hazard conditions. The rank distribution for this scenario (Figure  34 ) shows a modest departure from strict monotonic decay at intermediate ranks, consistent with the increased competition between candidate destinations discussed below in relation to Middle Centre (MC). Although the interacting hazards produce more complex movement patterns, the same behavioural mechanisms remain evident throughout the simulation.
 Fig. 31 Full size image Compound flooding scenario combining riverine and coastal hazards across five days. Location classes follow Figure 2.
 One notable feature is the population trajectory observed at Middle Centre (MC). MC’s flood level peaks at Level 1 between hours 24–66 and fully recedes to Level 0 by approximately hour 72. Across the 50-replica ensemble, MC’s population rises rapidly during the initial evacuation phase, peaking at \(24.14 \pm 0.08\) % of the total scenario population at 24 hours, coinciding with the onset of its own flood exposure. As MC remains at risk, displaced agents progressively vacate it in favour of the persistently safe TR, reducing its population by \(9.64 \pm 0.11\) percentage points to a trough of \(14.50 \pm 0.08\) % at 66 hours, immediately before local recession. MC therefore functions as a temporary secondary refuge under compound flooding: it initially absorbs a large share of evacuees from the fully flooded coastal and river-adjacent towns, redistributes them to TR during its own period of flood exposure, and regains population only after its flood level recedes. This sequential use of two refuges explains the comparatively low peak concentration of displaced populations at TR in this scenario despite the compound event producing among the highest overall displacement. Future extensions of DFlee could incorporate additional representations of infrastructure accessibility, dynamic destination attractiveness, and adaptive decision-making to better capture complex multi-hazard interactions.

 Appendix E sensitivity analysis results
 This appendix presents the complete results of the global sensitivity analysis (GSA) summarised in the Cross-Scenario Comparison. The analysis was performed using the EasyVVUQ framework to quantify the influence of behavioural and flood-related parameters on flood-induced displacement across the four flooding scenarios. Four uncertain parameters were considered: default_movechance , representing the baseline probability of movement; awareness_level , controlling agents’ awareness of neighbouring destinations; flood_move_scale , modifying movement decisions under flooding; and flood_severity_scale , controlling the influence of local flood severity on displacement generation and movement.
 Table  9 summarises the uncertain parameters together with their baseline values, sampling ranges, and probability distributions. The cumulative number of displaced individuals ( displaced_from_origin ) was selected as the model output, and first-order Sobol indices were computed to quantify the contribution of each parameter to the output variance. Figures  39 , 40 , 41 , 42 present the complete sensitivity analysis results for the Minor Riverine, Major Riverine, Coastal, and Compound flooding scenarios, respectively. For each scenario, panel (a) shows the temporal evolution of the first-order Sobol indices, while panel (b) presents the corresponding uncertainty envelope (ensemble mean \(\pm 1\) standard deviation).
 Table 9 Uncertain input parameters for the global sensitivity analysis. Each parameter was assigned an independent uniform distribution over the stated range. Baseline values correspond to those used in the scenario simulations reported in Table 4. The parameter space was sampled using a full-tensor third-order Stochastic Collocation expansion with Gauss quadrature (four nodes per dimension), yielding \(4^4 = 256\) model evaluations per flooding scenario. Full size table The sensitivity analysis reveals clear differences in parameter importance across the four flooding scenarios. In the Minor Riverine scenario (Figure  39 ), displacement dynamics are primarily governed by the behavioural parameter default_movechance , whose first-order Sobol index increases steadily throughout the simulation and reaches approximately 0.8 by the final simulation day. In contrast, the influence of flood_severity_scale and flood_move_scale decreases over time, indicating that displacement under relatively mild flooding is largely controlled by baseline mobility behaviour.
 A different sensitivity structure emerges under more severe flooding conditions. In the Major Riverine, Coastal, and Compound flooding scenarios (Figures  40 , 41 , 42 ), flood_severity_scale becomes one of the dominant contributors to output variance throughout much of the simulation, demonstrating that hydrological processes play an increasingly important role as flood severity increases. Although behavioural parameters continue to influence movement decisions, their relative contribution decreases compared with the Minor Riverine scenario.
 The uncertainty envelopes exhibit a consistent pattern across the four scenarios. Minor Riverine flooding produces the narrowest uncertainty band and the smallest displaced population, whereas the Major Riverine, Coastal, and Compound flooding scenarios exhibit progressively wider uncertainty envelopes associated with larger displacement events. This pattern indicates that uncertainty arising from flood-related processes increases with flood severity.
 Overall, the global sensitivity analysis demonstrates that DFlee exhibits physically interpretable and consistent parameter sensitivities across a range of flood hazards. Behavioural mobility parameters dominate displacement under relatively mild flooding, whereas flood-specific parameters account for an increasing proportion of output variance as hazard severity increases. These findings indicate that the model responds consistently to changing hazard conditions and support its ability to represent heterogeneous flood-induced displacement processes across a broad range of flooding scenarios.

 Appendix F ODD protocol for DFlee
 This appendix provides an ODD (Overview, Design Concepts, and Details) protocol 62,63 of DFlee to support reproducibility and facilitate comparison with other agent-based models.
 Purpose
 DFlee (Disaster Flee) is an agent-based model designed to simulate flood-induced displacement, including evacuation, temporary displacement, and return-to-origin. The model extends the Flee framework by incorporating flood-specific behavioural mechanisms that allow agents to respond dynamically to evolving flood conditions. The primary objective is to explore how flood severity, spatial configuration, and network accessibility influence population movements during flood events and to support humanitarian planning through scenario analysis.
 Entities, state variables, and scales
 Agents
 Each agent is characterised by its current location, home location, and displacement status (resident, displaced, or returned). Agent decisions are influenced by a configurable awareness parameter that determines the extent of information available about neighbouring locations and therefore affects destination selection and movement decisions.
 Locations
 Locations represent towns or settlements connected through a transportation network. Each location contains information on its coordinates, population, flood level, and location type. Locations serve both as places of residence and potential destinations for displaced populations. As flood conditions evolve, locations may transition between safe, at-risk, flooded, and submerged states, influencing population movements throughout the simulation. Flood levels vary over time and directly affect both evacuation decisions and destination attractiveness.
 Spatial scale
 The environment is represented as a graph consisting of locations (nodes) connected by transportation routes (edges). Route distances influence destination attractiveness and movement decisions. The framework can be applied to networks of varying size and complexity, ranging from simplified synthetic scenarios to real-world case studies.
 Temporal scale
 Time advances in discrete simulation steps. At each timestep, flood conditions, agent decisions, population movements, and return processes are updated. The duration and number of timesteps depend on the scenario being analysed.
 Process overview, scheduling, and design concepts
 At each simulation timestep, DFlee updates flood conditions and location attractiveness, evaluates evacuation and return decisions, executes movements through the transportation network, and records simulation outputs. The model assumes that individuals seek to minimise exposure to flood hazards while preferring accessible and comparatively safe destinations. Population-level displacement patterns emerge from the aggregate behaviour of individual agents, while stochastic movement decisions capture variation in risk perception and response timing.
 Adaptation
 Agents continuously adapt their behaviour in response to changing flood conditions. As flood severity increases, evacuation becomes more likely; as conditions improve, return-to-origin becomes possible. When forecasting is enabled, agents may also adapt their decisions according to anticipated future flood conditions.
 Emergence
 Population-level displacement patterns emerge from the aggregate behaviour of individual agents. No central coordination mechanism determines population movements.
 Objectives
 Agents seek to reduce exposure to flood hazards by relocating to safer destinations and subsequently returning home once conditions improve.
 Stochasticity
 Movement decisions include probabilistic components to represent variation in risk perception, response timing, and behavioural uncertainty among individuals. Consequently, agents exposed to similar flood conditions may not make identical movement decisions.
 Observation
 Model outputs include population distributions, evacuation flows, return flows, destination selection patterns, stylised-fact validation metrics, and computational performance indicators.
 Initialisation and input data
 At the beginning of each simulation, agents are assigned to locations according to population data, transportation routes are established, and scenario-specific flood trajectories are loaded. All agents begin in their home locations.
 DFlee uses external datasets describing Population distributions; Location networks and transportation routes; Flood conditions over time; and Scenario-specific simulation parameters.
 For empirical applications, the model can also incorporate observed displacement information, such as data from the International Organization for Migration (IOM) Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM).
 Behavioural submodels
 Flood evolution
 Flood conditions evolve throughout the simulation according to scenario-specific input data. Flood levels directly influence both evacuation behaviour and destination attractiveness.
 Evacuation decision
 Evacuation decisions are probabilistic rather than threshold-based. Each agent is assigned a movement probability that depends on local conditions. Under normal circumstances, agents follow a baseline movement probability. When flood rules are activated, flood-level-specific movement probabilities modify this baseline behaviour, increasing the likelihood of evacuation as flood severity rises. When enabled, forecasting mechanisms allow agents to incorporate anticipated future flood conditions into movement decisions.
 Destination selection
 When agents decide to evacuate, potential destinations are evaluated according to their relative attractiveness. Destination attractiveness depends on factors such as safety, accessibility, distance, and current flood conditions. Flood-specific location weights dynamically reduce the attractiveness of increasingly flooded destinations. Destination attractiveness also decays with distance from the agent’s current location (Equation 2), so that nearer safe locations are preferred and unnecessary long-distance displacement is avoided.
 Return decision
 Displaced agents may return to their home locations when flood conditions improve and the location is perceived as safe. Return decisions are therefore driven primarily by changes in flood risk and perceived safety. To maintain computational tractability and support large-scale scenario analysis, the current implementation does not explicitly model post-disaster recovery processes such as housing habitability, infrastructure reconstruction, utility restoration, or damage assessment.
 Movement
 Agents move between connected locations through the transportation network. Route accessibility, travel distance, and destination attractiveness influence movement patterns. Population counts are updated after each movement step, allowing the model to track evacuation, displacement, and return dynamics over time.
 Validation
 DFlee is evaluated using a two-stage validation framework.
 First, empirical validation is conducted using the 2022 Bauchi flood in Nigeria, where simulated displacement patterns are compared against observations from the IOM DTM. Second, behavioural validation is performed using stylised facts reported in the flood-displacement literature, including proximity-based destination choice, prompt post-flood return behaviour, and heterogeneous evacuation timing.
 Together, these validation approaches provide evidence of external validity and support the behavioural plausibility of DFlee, demonstrating that the model can reproduce key characteristics of flood-induced population displacement under both observed and synthetic flood conditions.
